This method creates a spot instance according to the specified parameters.

A Spot Instance is a specialized compute instance that allows you to access and utilize unused instance capacity at a steeply discounted rate. Spot price is charged on an hourly basis. 

To create a spot instance, follow these steps:

1. Select a data center using the `/v1/data-centers` endpoint. The data center determines the provider and location of the spot instance.

2. Select an available hardware configuration for the spot instance using the `/v1/spots-configs` endpoint.

3. Select an SSH key for the Linux spot instance using the `/v1/ssh-keys` endpoint.

4. Select an operating system using the `/v1/operating-systems` endpoint.

5. Choose one of the cloud network types: _multi-cloud, isolated,_ or _default_. Choose the _multi-cloud_ network type if you need to connect compute instances from different providers.

You may choose not to specify a security group. In this case, the spot instance will be added to the default security group.

A `price` field of a spot instance is not required. 

The spot instance market operates on a bidding system. Your specified price acts as your bid in this market. If your bid is higher than the current spot price, your instance request will likely be fulfilled. However, if the market price exceeds your bid, your instance may not be launched or could be terminated if already running.

description:
Register interest in the network quality of an application session and
obtain an opaque `id`. `applicationProfileId`, `applicationServer` and
`sink` are required; `device` is required only for a two-legged token.

See the API description for the parameter-driven functional cases (the
resolved identifier's trailing three digits select an open-ended vs a
time-bounded session, or a reserved CAMARA error).

**Network-initiated termination (CamaraSim model).** A `…001` identifier
creates an ordinary `ACTIVE` session, but the (simulated) network then
drops it early: after a short fixed grace the session is evicted and the
**terminal** `session-ended` CloudEvent (type
`org.camaraproject.session-insights.v0.session-ended`,
`data.terminationReason: NETWORK_TERMINATED`) is delivered to its `sink` —
fire-and-forget (`http://` sinks over raw TCP, `https://` sinks over a rustls
TLS session), so nothing delays the `201`. The
session's `sinkCredential` (stashed here — ACCESSTOKEN as `Bearer`, PLAIN as
`Basic`) authenticates the callback and is taken single-use (the event is
terminal). A concurrent
`deleteSession` that removed the session first makes this a no-op (exactly
one terminal event fires).

**Session expiry (CamaraSim model).** A time-bounded session (any
non-`…000`, non-`…001` tail, so it has an `expiresAt`) runs to that instant,
then an async expiry timer scheduled here evicts it and delivers the
**terminal** `session-ended` CloudEvent (`data.terminationReason:
SESSION_EXPIRED`) to its `sink` — same fire-and-forget transport and
`sinkCredential` auth (ACCESSTOKEN `Bearer` / PLAIN `Basic`) as the other
legs. The three terminal
transitions (`SESSION_DELETED` / `NETWORK_TERMINATED` / `SESSION_EXPIRED`)
are mutually exclusive — exactly one fires per session. An **open-ended**
session (`…000`/no-digits, no `expiresAt`) has no expiry timer.

description:
Issues one sandbox USD card to one of your customers. The card starts at `balance: 0` with
no spend limits, and every later call on this surface moves or gates that balance.

`customer.first_name`, `customer.last_name` and `customer.email` are required; the customer
is validated and then **not stored** — no name or email is persisted on the card, so a
leaked card id carries no PII with it. `reference` is yours, unique per business (a repeat
returns `409 duplicate_reference`), and defaults to the card id. `currency` may only be
`USD`; sending anything else returns 400.

The three limits are optional at issue time and are set or cleared later on
`POST /cards/{id}/spend_limits`. They are per-card ceilings you choose, and no platform maximum
is applied to any single axis. FirstFlip's ceilings sit elsewhere: one on how many cards a key
may hold open, and one on what all your cards may spend together — both stated below and in
the authorization section.

FirstFlip's one cap on issuing is a count, not an amount: a key may hold **250 open cards**.
The 251st `POST /cards` answers `409 card_limit_reached` with `param: cards` and nothing moves;
closing a card frees a slot, so a healthy integration is never locked out. Resending the same
`Idempotency-Key` is not a new card and is not counted.

The response shows `number_last4`, `expiry_month` and `expiry_year`. Those are minted here
for shape only — this card has no issuer, no full PAN and no CVV, and `sandbox.real_card`
says so on every answer. Requires an `Idempotency-Key` header.

Live mode: a live key is refused here before the body is read — issuing a real card needs the
cardholder rail FirstFlip has not built, so this answers `403 live_precondition_unmet` with
`param: cardholder`. No card is minted, and the refusal is what your key replays.

description:
Creates a Trust Domain — a group of devices on the subscriber's home
network sharing a common access policy — for one of the caller's
services. The caller submits a `TrustDomainCreate` (a `serviceId`, a
human-readable `name`, an `enabled` flag, and 1–4 `accessDetails`); the
simulator mints a server-assigned `trustDomainId`, stores the Trust
Domain in memory, and returns the full `TrustDomain` (`201`).

Three control planes drive the outcome (docs/DESIGN.md §7):

1. **The token subject** — a reserved error suffix on the authenticated
   identity selects the canonical CAMARA error (an account-level plane,
   checked first, mirroring `getServices`/`getService`).
2. **Request validation** — a missing/blank/oversized `name`, a missing
   `enabled`, a missing/malformed `serviceId`, an `accessDetails` that is
   empty or longer than 4, or an entry whose `accessType` is unknown, is
   not one this provider advertises (see
   `GET /trust-domains/capabilities`), or lacks its variant's required
   keys → `400 INVALID_ARGUMENT`.
3. **Store state** — the `trustDomainId` is derived from the
   `(serviceId, name)` pair, so creating a Trust Domain with the same
   `name` for the same `serviceId` collides → `409` (duplicate name for
   service).
